newsitem.title: GERMANY: Krupp, Thyssen seek steel pact as job fears grow.
newsitem.headline: Krupp, Thyssen seek steel pact as job fears grow.

text.p: One day after German industrial giant Thyssen vowed to fend off a hostile takeover by rival Fried. Krupp AG, the two companies said on Wednesday they would talk about forming a joint steel group which would be one of the world's largest.

Krupp and Thyssen said in a joint statement that they would hold eight days of talks aimed at a steel cooperation agreement. If successful, the talks would void Krupp's 13.6 billion mark ($8 billion) bid for Thyssen.
But if they failed to reach a pact in the agreed time, the two would return to their original positions, meaning Krupp could renew its generous offer to Thyssen shareholders.

In a meeting with Thyssen chairman Dieter Vogel and North Rhine-Westphalia state premier Johannes Rau, the ambitious Krupp chairman Gerhard Cromme appears to have won at least a week to persuade them cooperation makes sense.

The possibility of a merger in the German steel industry, which is based in North Rhine-Westphalia, has raised the prospect of heavy job losses at a time when unemployment is at its highest since 1933.
Underscoring the importance of preserving jobs, the Bild newspaper quoted Chancellor Helmut Kohl as urging the two companies to "live up to their total responsibilities".
"In the interest of those employed by both companies and in the interest of the economic climate in our country, the issue is to find a reasonable solution," said Kohl.
Economics minister Guenter Rexrodt said the talks between Krupp and Thyssen could help to boost the industry's international competitiveness.
"The two want to reach the goal of long-term competitiveness on their own ... and have not sought state subsidies, as is often the case in other places," he said.
Thousands of Thyssen steel workers decided to return to work on Wednesday after stopping production for two days. But they worried about their jobs as they awaited the outcome of the talks.
"The problems won't just be wiped off the table. We are watching this process critically," said Dieter Kroll, who heads an employees' council at unit Thyssen Stahl.

Newspaper editorials criticised the job cuts likely to result from a merger. But the two steel makers said in their joint statement that they had common problems that could be better solved by a larger entity.

A larger company might find it easier to cut the chronic overcapacity seen as one of the European steel industry's main impediments. High production costs in Germany are also a problem shared by both companies.
A wedding of the their steel operations would produce one of Europe's largest producers in tonnage output, in the same league with British Steel and France's Usinor Sacilor.

"A future-oriented concept, which was repeatedly considered in the past and has already led to successful joint ventures in the steel business, could solve the difficulties that both companies have in the steel sector," the joint statement said.
"This could lead on a partnership basis to a steel enterprise that takes a leading position in international rankings," it said.

On Tuesday Krupp launched a hostile bid for Thyssen, offering to pay 435 marks a share, or a premium of some 25 percent on Monday's closing. Shares were suspended from official trade on Tuesday and Wednesday but traded actively on the unofficial grey market.
But a Krupp spokesman said: "We do not yet own a single Thyssen share, and do not have a claim on any holding."
The tender offer would become valid only when Krupp filed the necessary disclosure statements and had made its presentation to banks, he told Reuters.

The Handelsblatt business daily noted Cromme had already met similar worker resistance in past efforts to reduce manufacturing capacity and in its 1991 takeover of the Hoesch group. "In both cases he won. Now the man of action Cromme wants to crack the toughest nut of all," it said. REUTER
